extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, publishers, and readers interested in research integrity / academic publishing
extracted.subtask_description: A news report about Frontiers retracting 122 articles after uncovering a network that undermined peer review; discusses causes (undisclosed conflicts, citation manipulation), publisher responses, and wider industry implications. Useful for readers tracking retractions and research-integrity practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrity of the peer review process
rubrics_metrics.description: Identified this article as one for which the integrity of the peer review process has been undermined, resulting in the loss of confidence in the article’s findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The publisher issued identical notices stating peer‑review integrity was compromised; when the review process is undermined, the publisher may retract even if it cannot determine who specifically was aware or involved. This is treated as sufficient cause for loss of confidence in findings and retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of conflicts of interest in peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Undisclosed conflicts of interest in the peer review (e.g., reviewer and author had previously coauthored a paper together).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigations flagged instances where reviewers/handling editors had past coauthorship with authors (example: reviewer Muhammad Mohsin). Publishers should verify and require accurate COI statements for reviewers and editors; undisclosed COIs can invalidate peer review and justify retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation manipulation / citation collusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors and editors engaged in 'manipulating citations' as an unethical action tied to the network.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patterns of inflated or reciprocated citations that appear to be coordinated are treated as misconduct. Distinguishing legitimate citation of relevant work from manipulative citation is necessary; publishers and investigators should look for patterns across publications and collections (e.g., Research Topics/special issues).

rubrics_metrics.name: Detection and investigation of collusive author/editor networks
rubrics_metrics.description: A broad and sophisticated network of about 35 authors were potentially colluding over a very large number of journals and published papers, linking thousands of articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research integrity teams should map coauthor and reviewer networks across submissions and publications to detect coordinated behavior. Frontiers identified >4,000 linked articles and began bulk retractions after identifying the network; network detection can trigger retrospective audits of many papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audit of authors' prior submissions, publications, and coauthor networks
rubrics_metrics.description: After a tip, the research integrity team began investigating all the authors’ previous submissions, publications, and coauthor networks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proactive, retrospective audits of an author’s prior work and collaboration patterns can reveal systemic problems beyond a single paper. This may include reviewing prior reviewer assignments, editorial roles, and coauthorship ties to assess scope of misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retraction when scientific integrity cannot be guaranteed
rubrics_metrics.description: Misconduct was significant enough to determine that the scientific integrity of the article cannot be guaranteed, prompting retraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the investigation cannot determine whether every author/editor/reviewer was aware or involved, a finding that integrity cannot be assured is sufficient to retract. Retraction is used as the remedy when confidence in findings is lost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publisher sharing investigation methodology and cross-publisher collaboration
rubrics_metrics.description: The publisher’s research integrity team said it is willing to share details and the methodology of their investigation with other publishers and is a member of the STM Hub.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sharing methods, data, and lists of implicated papers with other publishers aids industry-wide detection and cleanup. Membership in cooperative platforms (e.g., STM Hub) facilitates cross-publisher action on networks and paper mills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of AI tools to verify reviewer/editor conflicts
rubrics_metrics.description: Frontiers has an artificial intelligence review system for submitted manuscripts, which now includes verification of the reviewers’ and handling editors’ conflict of interest statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers may deploy AI to screen reviewer/editor identities and COIs, but the article and comments note skepticism: AI must be complemented by robust human oversight and transparent vetting to avoid false negatives/positives and bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial independence and the ability of editors to reject submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Anecdotal reports that editors were not allowed to reject papers and that acceptance could be forced (i.e., editors overruled), undermining gatekeeping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial processes should empower editors to reject unsuitable work. Anti-patterns include institutional pressure to accept papers for rapid throughput or revenue, which can enable poor-quality or fraudulent publications; robust editorial independence is a quality criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency of review and retraction processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Calls for the publisher to clarify its review process and to share details of how the investigation took place; demand for clearer reasoning in retraction notices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers should publicly describe their review workflows, criteria for acceptance/rejection, and publish clear, specific retraction notices and investigation summaries (or at least summaries of methods) to build trust and enable external verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refunding article processing charges (APCs) for retracted papers (accountability measure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggestions that journals should refund all fees for retracted papers to hold publishers accountable for poor gatekeeping and harming authors’ reputations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a proposed accountability mechanism discussed in comments. Guidance notes tradeoffs and counterarguments: refunds could create perverse incentives for fraudsters or fail to deter repeat offenders; policy design should consider effects on victims and incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions for repeat offenders (blacklisting / preventing further submissions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals to prevent repeat fraudulent authors from publishing (e.g., blacklisting authors with many retractions) as a way to deter misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sanctioning repeat offenders can reduce recidivism but raises procedural fairness concerns. Implementations require clear evidence standards, due process, and coordination across publishers to be effective and equitable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case-by-case assessment of coauthorship as a conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Debate over whether prior coauthorship between reviewer and author should be treated as an absolute deal‑breaker, noting small fields where collaborators are few.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conflict-of-interest policies should account for field size and context; blanket prohibitions can be impractical in tight-knit fields. Investigations should evaluate the degree of relationship and potential for biased review rather than automatically disqualifying any prior coauthorship without context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing legitimate citation behavior from collusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Concerns that normal citation practices (e.g., sharing output with colleagues, citing friends’ relevant work) can be misinterpreted as collusion if detected as networked citation patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessors should evaluate intent, relevance, and patterns (e.g., excessive reciprocal citation, irrelevant self-citation clusters) to differentiate legitimate scholarly citation from manipulative schemes. Blanket metrics can misclassify normal scholarly behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibility of researchers/consumers to critically read and evaluate papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Argument that 'the onus is on scientists to read and understand papers, not blindly accept that
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers and other readers should not treat peer review as an absolute certification; critical evaluation of methods and claims remains necessary. This reduces overreliance on journal reputation as a proxy for quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain public, searchable records and lists of affected/retracted papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Provision of a list of forthcoming retractions by the publisher and Retraction Watch's database and invitation to report missing retractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keeping accessible lists or databases of retractions and implicated authors (and sharing spreadsheets or datasets) supports transparency, helps other publishers check overlap, and notifies readers and citers of affected work.
